This paper introduces a formalized K-Nearest-Neighbors (KNN) interference regression framework, which extends the standard approach developed by Muennig and others (2011). We establish properties of this KNN model and derive a large-sample theory for the difference-in-means estimator, analyzing its bias specifically. To address these complexities and handle potential issues with the difference-in-means estimator, we develop a novel detector utilizing the generalized linear laws of motion (GLLM) technique. Applied to a study involving students and tutoring sessions, our results indicate that the difference-in-means estimator produces severely biased results due to interference. In contrast, the proposed GLLMs-based detector successfully identifies interference presence without exhibiting bias itself, offering a significant improvement over previous methods.

We investigate neutrino emissions resulting from dark matter (DM) annihilation within the dense environment of the Sun, specifically focusing on the neutrino sectors involving the neutral components of scalar and complex scalar fields coupled to DM through a universal pseudoscalar interaction. In this framework, we determine that the dominant dark matter Sun capture rate is governed by the spin-independent scattering cross section, whereas neutrino luminosity arises from contributions both proportional to and independent of the annihilation energy. Because dark matter Sun capture can be significantly more efficient than that of Earth, we propose that searching for these specific signals offers a powerful strategy for detecting this class of dark matter.

This study introduces ShapePipe, a pipeline designed to streamline shape measurements for diverse input data and detection methods while maintaining consistency across various sources. The primary objective is to facilitate the execution of cosmological investigations utilizing data from the UNIONS survey combined with photometric and spectroscopic insights from CFIS. Unions survey data encompasses optical imaging from four distinct telescops, covering a total area exceeding one square degree and reaching photometric limits of approximately 24.5 AB mag. Although this depth supports the capture of over ten million galaxies at redshifts below 1.5, achieving a $<1.5 \times$ magnitude limit is not sufficient on its own. To provide a robust framework for future cosmological research, we deliver open-source software that integrates multiple downstream data processing steps. Within this workflow, our specific contributions include data ingestion, catalog management, and the measurement of co-adding image shapes using consistent methodologies. We evaluate shape measurement consistency and apply our pipeline to a collection of group-galaxy pairs derived from the CFIS region to characterize potential systematics relevant to large-scale structure analysis using the UNIONS survey data.

The discovery of spin liquids in Heisenberg magnets has sparked intense research into the magnetism of these systems. This specific category of quantum ground states, where spins remain constantly fluctuating even at absolute zero, exhibits strikingly non-trivial entanglement structures. A particularly significant aspect involves the connection between geometric entanglement and the sign of the inter-spin exchange interaction. This connection can be established through either an indirect or a direct route. The indirect path entails analyzing how the exchange interaction influences the variational entanglement of individual spin states, whereas the indirect approach assesses how magnetic field adjustments modify this fundamental interaction. This work focuses on the latter method, specifically employing tensor network techniques to examine how an applied magnetic field modulates the exchange interaction in Heisenberg models. Our findings, which apply to both one- and two-dimensional Heisenberg systems, reveal that the exchange interaction is directly controlled by external fields and can switch from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic behaviors.

From January 2017 to June 2018, the LAMOST Time Domain (TD) project utilized the K1 and K2 single-fiber spectroscopic instruments to observe the sky, using the 1.26 m GOTO telescists to cover a total area of 22,000 deg$^2$. This specific study details preliminary findings from 44 plate exposures across 1,078 fields, collectively known as the K2 plates, which span a magnitude range of 5.5 to 18.9 in the SDSS g-rr' color-magnitude diagram (CMD) selection box. Utilizing an ensemble of 42 publicly available photometric datasets, we identified the precise coordinates and coordinates for over 30 million stars. By cross-referencing these positions against the Gaia EDR3 catalog, we determined coordinates and radial velocities for approximately 100 million stars with Gaia-derived proper motions and Galactocentric coordinates. Finally, using the machine-learning tool MCMG-MLP to classify variability, we identified roughly 100 million variable stars. The luminosity function analysis indicates that the majority of these variables belong to the Cepheid and RR Lyrae populations.

This work introduces TuRaN, a SRAM true random number generator that leverages energy efficiency principles. It begins by verifying the viability of supply voltage undervolting in SRAMs to reduce power consumption during cell read operations, while simultaneously demonstrating that this voltage variation amplifies data unpredictability. By utilizing this heightened variability in emerging states, unexpected outcomes emerge, serving as highly dependable sources of true randomness. Our approach offers an innovative strategy for generating random numbers and stands as a significant contribution to energy-conscious security solutions. A dedicated hardware unit was constructed and evaluated across multiple advanced technology nodes, confirming that supply voltage undervolting indeed increases yield uncertainty and that this technique successfully delivers a fast, high-quality PR stream of randomness.

We have created a simulation framework for single-electron resistive switches utilizing molecular break-junction structures. This framework employs *ab initio* non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) methodology to analyze the resistance states and the transition between them in switch designs featuring gold electrodes paired with benzene-1,4-bis(thiophenol) or gold nanocrystal-oxide nanoparticle molecules. We utilize *ab initio* density functional theory (DFT) for all electronic structure calculations. By integrating these computational techniques with experimental data from molecular self-assembly processes, we validate our resistance values and Nequilibrium Green's function results. A novel non-equilibrium Green's function method specific to resistance-state switching is introduced, designed to handle the stochastic detachment and rearrangement of molecules or nanoparticles within the switch architecture.

This work introduces a novel strategy for the causal depiction of massless one-loop scalar Feynman diagrams featuring arbitrary dimensions, regulator order, and massless internal/external propagators. While this approach aligns with the results derived by Bloch-Zwanziger, it achieves it through a distinct methodology. Furthermore, the study generalizes their findings to the multi-loop scenario and proves a unique, algorithmic, and rigorous mapping between causal depiction land-scape and Landau manifold. Finally, the authors present an efficient algorithm capable of evaluating massless scalar multi-loop integrands and provide comparative data between their algorithm's performance and that of the Package ULRIC multi-loop numerical integration software.

This study examines phase transitions between hadronic and quark matter within hybrid stars by applying an MIT quark mass operator of 36 MeV. The proposed model incorporates a hadronic framework based on the $\sigma$-$\omega$-$\rho$ theory and utilizes pressure continuity at the phase boundary, guided by Gibbs' criteria. Analysis reveals that increasing the value of critical chemical potential enhances the soft regions of the equation of state, thereby softening the stellar behavior. This study introduces a quantum master equation framework to characterize the quantum statistics of a dilute gas of laser-cooled atoms trapped within a dissipative optical lattice. Our analysis indicates that, unlike traditional systems, the probability distribution for atomic occupancy follows a super-Poissonian statistic featuring a distinct bimodal structure. This behavior suggests the presence of effective two-level dynamics in the laser-cooled, lattice-confined atoms. Furthermore, the paper identifies two strategic approaches to manipulate the ratio of modal heights within this bimodal distribution, offering a pathway to engineer the quantum statistical properties of atoms in such lattices.

This study examines the network structure of the cryptocurrency trading market by analyzing data from major exchanges, beginning with an overview of the evolution of the trading entity network over the last four years. It reveals a small-world characteristic marked by a degree exponent of 2.36, a 6.28 average path length, and a clustering coefficient of 0.49. Furthermore, the research develops a methodological framework for investigating both pairwise and multi-asset relationships within the trading network, achieving the following insights: first, high-order interactions consistently exhibit stronger seasonality than pairwise dynamics, with cycles extending up to approximately 8 days; second, trading links across order heights display varying resilience, noting a shift in the core trading asset towards more volatile cryptocurrencies as time progresses, and observing that trading links in deeper orders are more prone to long-range correlations compared to those at the queue top.

Acid rain is a significant environmental concern, and its formation relies on the nucleation of sulfuric acid and water molecules. While QUAPF successfully highlights the critical role of zero-point motion in enhancing cluster accuracy, further refinements through quantum simulations remain necessary to fully capture these effects.

A key unresolved issue regarding deep learning's success involves understanding how models learn interpretable features and structured representations, including the role of representation complexity in training dynamics. This study examines these mechanisms from the perspective of representational Geometric Complexity (RGC), a metric measuring the geometric learning complexity of a model's representation space. We investigate RGC in both supervised classification and unsupervised self-supervised learning. Our findings reveal that although trained models exhibit low RGC—indicating the inherent simplicity of their discovered representations, RGC also serves as a predictor for representation quality. Furthermore, RGC acts effectively as a regularizer, enhancing robustness and training stability in deep learning frameworks.

An experimental approach to directly extract Wilson coefficients for the decays $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ is outlined, focusing on four key observables: the branching ratio, the forward-backward asymmetry, the polar angle asymmetries, and the Bo$Bo$ asymmetry. It is demonstrated that the direct determination of the parameters $a_b$ and $b_b$ becomes feasible by analyzing the branching ratio alongside the real component of the relevant Wilson coefficient, whereas the imaginary component of the $b_b$ parameter can be measured using forward-backward asymmetries or the Bo$Bo$ asymmetry terms. Furthermore, this study evaluates the sensitivity of the proposed method against standard approaches that rely on taking limits where q² approaches zero or the B$B$ system resonance.

Automated essay scoring is a well-established area of Natural Language Processing (NLP) that focuses on analyzing text to evaluate a specific attribute, most commonly linguistic proficiency. This research explores a key challenge in this field: expanding limited labeled datasets to train robust deep learning models for effective paper grading. We investigate data augmentation techniques, specifically back-translation, and assess their impact on transformer-based automated scoring systems. Using the Facebook BART model for our experiments on the combined IEF and Duolango English Language Education datasets, we achieved significant performance gains by augmenting the data with English translations of Spanish essays. These results demonstrate a boost in correlation metrics from a baseline of 0.4933 to 0.5183 using Pearson correlation.

Existing copula-based models for capturing marginal effects are scarce. This study introduces a novel class of such models by applying a one-to-one transformation to an equal-energy copula. We offer closed-form expressions for the transformed variables' density function, moments, and tail dependence coefficients, while also estimating these via Maximum Likelihood and providing the corresponding Fisher information matrix. Finally, we apply this new modeling framework to monthly S&P500 returns, estimating parameters for eight distinct copula families to calculate moment and tail dependence results that include a transformation; these results are then compared against those derived using a direct two-parameter normal-copula model.

This research investigates the movement of individuals across social strata over multiple generations using a quantitative, dynamic framework. Our model extends a previously established qualitative dynamic framework by incorporating specific distributional assumptions regarding parental and external influences on offspring outcomes, allowing for the simulation of multiple generations to examine the persistence of intergenerational mobility. By fitting the model's assumptions to historical opportunity structures and data from the British Opportunity Survey (BOS), we determine the specific parameters through simulation until the resulting steady-state distribution aligns with observed reality. Our results, derived from this data-aligned model, explore the distinct impacts of external factors and parental behavior on social mobility persistence and analyze how shifting environmental conditions influence the distribution of opportunities and mobility rates across different time periods.

We introduce a modified RingCT variant called "Deleged RingCT," which reduces computational overhead for transaction validation from $O(n)$ to $O(1)$ by eliminating the need for a full Proof of Work (PoW) on every transaction. In this protocol, transactions are grouped into chains secured by a single Delegation PoW provided by a participant at the transaction initiation. Validation then depends on verifying cumulative proofs rather than individual ones for each step. This approach ensures an energy consumption of only $O(\epsilon)$ per transaction, where $\epsilon$ is the minimum difficulty required by Bitcoin, effectively making the cost negligible. Although we address potential liveness concerns associated with untrusted initiators, we also outline a path toward resolving this issue.

We introduce a general framework addressing linear equations within data-structured spaces, where each operation corresponds to a specific computational "step." This paper investigates key properties related to spatial complexity—specifically data structures and memory usage—within this new context. Applying the space-time complexity constraints previously suggested by Frieze, Kannan, and Smith (FKS) for convex programming, we demonstrate that these space tough limits apply universally across all space-efficient data structures. Furthermore, we propose several new space-efficient structures for affine and positive cones, which currently achieve the best known time- and space-complexity balances for these specific geometric primitives.

Recent research indicates that core NLP tasks are undergoing a renaissance, with significant strides in areas like coreference resolution, sentiment analysis, and statistical machine translation. This paper addresses HeTree, a secondary corpus of Hebrew sentence trees developed through annotated sentences from online news sources using the annotation protocols of the Universal Hebrew Treebank. Recognizing that the TreeBank's coverage extends back over a decade and the newer HeTree corpus pushes to present-day data, we have integrated these resources through several augmentation strategies. To further enrich this combined data, we have introduced a new, large-scale Hebrew corpus consisting of parsed sentences from multiple distant parsing systems. The effectiveness of this enhanced data is demonstrated by training parsers on it, which results in improved performance metrics.

Modern data-driven modeling and design are rapidly transforming engineering, a field where artificial intelligence and machine learning are driving breakthroughs in creating robust new algorithms. A key challenge remains the lack of adequate data for training these models across complex systems with varying operating conditions, often resulting from sparse recordings under extreme states. To address this, we introduce a novel "collaborative data-driven modeling" algorithm designed to merge training datasets from multiple individual models. By rephrasing the problem as an optimization task and employing an alternating optimization strategy, we achieve global optimality through alternately solving two subproblems. Our approach is supported by a rigorous error analysis of the resulting cross-trained models and demonstrated via a case study involving multi-input nonlinear systems with differing unmeasured excitation levels.

This paper introduces an innovative degree-degree correlation model for Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes designed specifically for the binary deletion channel (CDC). Our proposed model, which links the degrees of adjacent vertices within the code's graph, demonstrates a strong correlation with decoding speed. We analyze correlations between node degrees and demonstrate that adopting our degree-degree correlation framework significantly enhances LDPC performance under CDC conditions. Results from both our new degree-degree correlation model and those examining neighboring nodes' min-rims confirm this significant improvement.

We introduce a novel approach for ensuring safety in linear systems subject to external disturbances and initial conditions, where the goal is to determine a predictive controller. This controller synthesizes a state feedback law capable of minimizing the largest possible perturbation required to keep system trajectories within the safe set, given dimensions of uncertainty. We label this metric as the "Safety Margin," demonstrate that it corresponds to a specific semi-definite programming problem, and show how to compute it efficiently. Furthermore, we discuss how this framework can be viewed as an extension of invariant set theory, noting that the maximum allowable disturbance under constraints equates to scenarios with no initial state and no control restrictions.

We demonstrate theoretically that an eavesdropper can successfully hack a decoy-state quantum key distribution system without needing full phase coherence, provided only partial phase randomization is used by the laser source. In this scenario, the information gain by the hacker exceeds the allowed quantum error tolerance, yet remains undetectable within bounds of the signal transmission quality. By bypassing a critical safety mechanism, such an attack allows the hacker to acquire excessive information which remains hidden from detection. We calculate an upper limit of 29.25% for data acquisition under these conditions and suggest new security verification criteria to mitigate this vulnerability and enhance overall protocol safety.

In this study, we analyze the dynamics of cold gas clumps resulting from shocks in the cosmic web using high-resolution, radiative-hydrodynamical simulations. Our work establishes a set of analytical formulas to characterize clump evolution throughout their growth and fragmentation processes. We find that an initial fragmentation process occurs rapidly within approximately $10^7$ years across all scenarios, regardless of whether magnetic fields or thermal conduction are present. Subsequent behavior diverges: with thermal conduction active, clumps merge over subsequent $10^7$ to $10^8$ years; otherwise, they remain isolated and do not merge within $10^9$ years. While the initial fragmentation timescale proves independent of a cluster's large-scale environment, the later growth phase—specifically the interval from $10^7$ to $10^8$ years—is heavily influenced by it. We developed an analytical model for the final size of these clumps that accurately aligns with simulation data, offering a method to determine the large-scale environmental factors by measuring the size of existing cold gas structures.

This review examines CP violation within the context of neutral B-meson decays, highlighting recent findings from experiments at the Tevatron, together with analytical predictions from the Standard Model. It also outlines prospects for future studies of the beauty quark sector using LHC experiments and the Tevatron, as well as plans for the distance-to-collision (d-to-p) experiments at LHC.

Driven by the massive scale of future 5G core networks (CN), which will render traditional manual administration impractical, this study introduces a framework leveraging Machine Learning (ML) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV). The proposed solution employs a self-configuration, self-optimizing, self-healing, and self-preserving (SSSHP) architecture, relying on four integrated modules: KPI & KQI Monitoring, Fault Detection & Diagnosis (FDD), KPI & Fault Prediction (FP), and Change Management (CM). Key innovations include a novel Fault Propagation (FP) algorithm utilizing supervised ML to bolster existing diagnostics, alongside a Change Management (CM) module designed to streamline the lifecycle of network function containers within the infrastructure. Performance was evaluated using both real 5G CN logs and synthetic data, demonstrating superior results from the new ML-based FDD component and validating the overall capability for robust key performance.

A significant challenge in text-to-speech synthesis is creating models that function without labeled audio data. This study introduces a zero-resource synthesis system utilizing a neural network trained on perceptual acoustic units. By defining input features based on a reduced set of acoustic units derived from transcript analysis, we train the model to generate speech. This training process is streamlined through the use of feature-level speaker and phoneme identification tags, which simplify both training and interpretation. To evaluate speech quality, we train the system on a large audio dataset containing labels for both phoneme and speaker identity.

This research addresses interval motion planning, a task involving the guidance of a dynamic system through a sequence of specified regions accounting for uncertainty. A primary difficulty lies in determining a single robust trajectory capable of guiding the system to these targets despite such unpredictability. To address this, we introduce a multi-stage optimization framework tailored for dynamic intervals that functions as a distributed, data-driven decomposition of the underlying non-convex problem. By incorporating tailored McCormick envelope relaxations, we ensure that each optimized sub-trajectory correctly represents the uncertainty evolution of the original path. Additionally, by formulating these regions adaptively based on system dynamics, our approach effectively mitigates the classic "pessimism" often associated with decoupling methods. Extensive experiments across various scenarios demonstrate that this optimization strategy successfully generates robust trajectories that achieve every planned target while substantially outperforming existing techniques in terms of planning efficiency and trajectory sharpness.

Recent research by Gour et al. (Gour, J. Phys. Math. Chem., 2020) examined the probabilistic conversion of quantum states under bipartite local operations and showed how the non-negativity of the R\'enyi divergence of order 2 ($R_2$) between arbitrary quantum states imposes an upper bound on the maximum probability of successful conversion. This limit, representing the best-probability achievable for creating a target state from a given initial one, was later analyzed using bipartite entanglement. This study extends those findings to single-qubit pure states, where we derive new constraints specific to $R_2$ that further lower that success probability bound. We demonstrate that these restrictions are stringent and widespread within the state space, leading to a significant reduction of the previously identified upper limit. Crucially, we reveal a direct relationship showing how this reduced probability correlates with the initial fidelity of the state pair.

This study investigates the motion of a shaking liquid within a cylindrical container, modeling it as a damped, forced simple pendulum. While exact solutions remain unattainable, we employ the perturbation method to construct a scaling argument. This approach demonstrates that the system's behavior is governed by the ratio between the driving acceleration and the fluid's natural gravity wave frequency, supplemented by a scaling factor for the container's free surface slope. Our analysis reveals that the resulting phase portraits are universally similar across different fluid types and container sizes, provided the scaling of the surface slope is applied. These findings were validated through experiments using water, alcohol, and coffee, with our theoretical predictions confirmed by numerical simulations.

Decentralized learning involves training machine learning models in a fully distributed setup across a network of agents connected in a general graph, where information exchange occurs only between neighboring nodes. This approach offers significant advantages in specific scenarios, such as reduced communication overhead and enhanced privacy. However, it also introduces vulnerabilities, as an adversary capable of manipulating data at a single node can bias the global model toward a specific local distribution. To address this, we introduce DR-DSGD, a novel distributed learning algorithm designed to be robust against the injection of adversarial data. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that DR-DSGD achieves an $\epsilon$-approximate global minimum within distribution-specific regret bounds. Comparative experiments between our method and baseline algorithms show significant improvements when facing distribution shift challenges.

We employ hydrodynamic attractors within non-linear relativistic non-equilibrium hydrodynamics to investigate the primordial development of the anisotropic energy density in relativistic nuclear collisions. This analysis demonstrates that, at a fixed time in the laboratory frame, the magnitude of the anisotropic energy density in the plane transverse to the beam direction exceeds its longitudinal component. Additionally, we derive the initial non-equilibrium energy distribution for particle production by formulating anisotropic expansion in terms of the ideal hydrodynamic conservation laws.

While high-velocity outflows are commonly observed in high-mass star formation, low-mass protostar outflows are typically slow, a disparity this study partially explains by highlighting the dominance of disk interference in low-mass systems versus direct penetration for high-mass ones. Using smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, we modeled a high-velocity protostellar jet intersecting with a low-mass disk at various angles to assess how effectively the jet can drive outflows directly. Our results indicate that a 1000 km/s jet impacts the disk with consistent force across all angles, generating vertical shocks that launch disk material into outflows regardless of the trajectory. Specifically, a perpendicular (90°) jet creates a prominent bow shock that generates a high-velocity core directly, whereas oblique injections transform into shock-heated, turbulent "halo" gas above the disk that dissipates kinetic energy into heat and turbulence, yielding a smoother overall velocity structure despite the driving impact. By simulating a mix of bow shocks (from near-perpendicular jets) and shock-heated turbulent halos (from misaligned jets) along the same ejection axis, we successfully replicate the characteristic fast inner and slow outer components of outflows commonly seen in low-mass star formation.

This study addresses the problem of balancing performance and saturation limits during the control design for constrained nonlinear systems. By employing the equilibrium concept from control theory, we establish a novel performance-at-safety (PAT-SAFE) framework. This approach determines a reference signal that equates the desired performance level with safety guarantees, ensuring that trajectories remain outside the region of saturation. To achieve this, we derive an invariant set complementary to the domain where saturation occurs and integrate it with a desired under-level set corresponding to specific performance criteria. The resulting control strategy, labeled simply as such for safety and performance (PAT-SAFE), generates the equilibrium signal directly. We provide sufficient topological requirements for achieving this balance under general constraints and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through two key scenarios: ensuring anti-windup protection in systems with integrators subject to input limits, and regulating position for mobile robots with bounded velocities.

This study presents general analytical conditions regarding the stability of semi-secret resonances caused by gravitational perturbations and solar radiation pressure (SRP) on small bodies within the asteroid belt. While the primary analysis relies on an approximated orbit model incorporating SRP via the $\beta$ parameter, results are validated through comparisons with numerical simulations of completely perturbed systems. We demonstrate that for asteroids with $\beta < 0.09$, stable resonance zones persist; in contrast, when $\beta$ exceeds this threshold, these zones become unstable.

We demonstrate that within certain tight-binding first-principles models of light-matter interaction, the optical response remains unchanged regardless of the specific gauge choice used to partition vector potentials between lattice sites. We further define the precise conditions under which gauge invariance holds and explain the underlying mechanism. Notably, this stability arises because the apparent gauge dependence resides solely in a term responsible for lattice charge transport; removing this dependence requires lattice sites to be electrically neutral in the presence of vector potentials. We establish that charge transport corresponds exactly to the condition of current conservation at every site when vector potentials are absent, confirming that measure invariance of the current equivalence class under gauge transformation is both necessary and sufficient. Finally, we clarify that gauge independence of optical responses is linked to the validity of the optical sum rule, which itself is a consequence of expressing electronic states in a specific gauge-invariant manner.

This study examines a configuration involving $m$ observations from one Cauchy population and another from the second population with $n$ observations. We introduce a specific transformation to these datasets to establish, for the location parameter of interest, an exact confidence interval for the case when the scale parameters are equal, as well as separate unequal confidence intervals. Additionally, we evaluate the accuracy of calculated intervals through mean squared error for the scale parameter estimator. To evaluate this, we utilize a confidence interval method based on a specific transformation of the data, specifically addressing a scenario with $m$ observations from one Cauchy population and $n$ observations from another. The work establishes an exact confidence interval for estimating the location parameter under conditions where scale parameters are equal, alongside distinct intervals for each when they differ. Basket studies are increasingly valuable in pharmaceuticals, allowing a single analysis assumption that patient subsets share a common treatment effect despite varying responses based on subgroup characteristics. This analysis often requires pooling data to achieve sufficient power, posing planning challenges in determining an adequate sample size a priori. To address this, we propose a Bayesian framework for sample size planning that evaluates the required number of participants by incorporating potential information borrowing among baskets and incorporating subgroups. Using a hierarchical model, we assume a unified baseline effect across subgroups within baskets while permitting varying individual responses. By integrating this effect with observed data, we can estimate treatment effects more precisely, influencing the sample size calculation accordingly. Employing a type II error probability criterion, we first calculate a baseline sample size ignoring borrowed data before refining it using posterior distributions that account for borrowing scenarios. Numerical examples demonstrate how acknowledging information borrowing can substantially reduce necessary recruitment, and further, we explore the impact of subsegments on both effect estimation accuracy and final sample size requirements.

This paper introduces a model prediction-based control scheme designed for high-precision motion systems, emphasizing high sampling rates, rigorous accuracy, and robustness. While traditional control approaches often struggle with precision limitations or inability to manage large dynamics, this proposed framework addresses these drawbacks by integrating robust control with Model Predictive Control (LMP). Specifically, sequential loop tightening (SLT) is employed through the calculation of terminal sets to enable predictive tightening. However, existing terminal set methodologies face constraints regarding model uncertainty and computational complexity. This study overcomes such restrictions by adopting a parallel bank of filters method within SLT, yielding improved terminal sets for LPV systems characterized by both large variations and extensive uncertainty margins. Simulation results validate the superior performance of this approach in motion control applications compared to current terminal set techniques.

Deep learning-based, self-supervised network approaches for image registration have recently garnered significant attention. Unlike traditional methods requiring manual labels, these techniques utilize partial ground truth data to bridge the gap to the fully supervised paradigm, demonstrating promising results even with substantial missing data. Nevertheless, most existing techniques, such as autoencoders and generative adversarial networks, either depend on fully or partially annotated target images or fail to account for how missing data influences feature extraction and loss calculation. To address this, we introduce PRNet, a fully self-supervised registration network designed to align two pairs of features, extracting only relevant data while ignoring missing portions. Unlike standard autoencoders that require labeled targets, PRNet utilizes an innovative cross-correlation mechanism within its U-Net architecture during a fully self-supervised framework to ignore discrepancies in missing areas. This approach maximizes structural similarity through cross-correlation while minimizing volume variance, ensuring robust alignment without human annotation. We evaluated PRNet using synthetic data with holes ranging from 20% to 80%, as well as on real MRI and CT datasets. Results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in fully self-supervised partial registration tasks.

In medical image analysis, instances of specific anatomical or pathological features are hard to annotate due to their sparse labeling and difficult segmentation. Traditional instance segmentation networks fail because they lack the generation capability to annotate unlabeled new images. This study introduces an innovative Cyclic Discrete GAN (CDCG) framework that enables instance segmentation across diverse imaging modalities. Starting with labeled data from a source domain, we extract features and generate synthetic instances within those labeled images using a discrete GAN. Subsequently, a cyclic translation process is applied to map these generated instances into an unlabeled target domain, effectively creating new training data. These augmented data are then employed to fine-tone the segmentation network. Experimental results demonstrate that this method enhances the source domain network's capability to segment the target domain, yielding superior performance over current state-of-the-art methods.

Neural networks for neural network control have recently gained attention due to their superior capability in performing long-term predictions of dynamical systems. Building on this, we introduce an improvement to Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) that utilizes learnable, radially basis function (RBF) kernel feature mapping. We demonstrate that this enhancement significantly boosts prediction accuracy. Specifically, this approach outperforms standard RNN action prediction and matches the performance of densely connected neural networks with RBF kernels. Additionally, we assess the proposed architecture using two distinct state transition environments to establish performance baselines and evaluate the benefits of this approach.

Neural smoothing is a technique that uses convolutional neural networks to create smooth, differential-renderable 3D point clouds. However, existing approaches often produce non-differential surfaces because they fail to account for local geometry or global topology when selecting neighborhood points. To solve this, we introduce Neural Smoothing with Uniquely Transformable Convolutional networks (NUTC), a new method that ensures locally unique smoothness under transformations. Our approach transforms the neighborhood point selection process into a learning task: we train a network to map any neighborhood around a center point into Euclidean space using topologically valid embeddings, such as the Hilbert curve or space-filling function. These embeddings guarantee that neighboring points under different local rigid transformations map to nearly identical positions in feature space. We prove that our method enables the point cloud center's local smoothness to remain differentiable regardless of how their 3D coordinates transform. Translational invariance allows us to learn a single set of neighborhood weights for any location, while we analytically derive transformation-dependent but topologically consistent target locations for those points. Transformations at specific locations can be predicted by a neural network that learns the local rigid transformation field. We demonstrate theoretically and empirically that our learning-based geometry embedding effectively handles local rigid transformations, maintaining smoothness properties without loss of accuracy under transformation.

This study examines the network performance of Frequency-Linear Chirped Massively Parallel FMCW (SLAP FMCW) radars, which employ the slotted ALOHA and CSMA medium access control protocols. Since these media access methods depend on chirps, we investigate their impact, alongside collision probability, on network throughput. To analyze interference resulting from concurrent transmissions, a stochastic geometry framework was employed to compute collision probabilities within SLAP FMCW systems operating under both unsaturated and saturated network conditions. To validate the proposed theoretical outcomes, we implemented a network simulator using Python. Finally, comparative performance graphs were generated, contrasting the different transmission schemes and their respective performances.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Inference (TKGI) aims to forecast missing facts in Temporal Knowledge Databases (TKGs), which consist of entity-relation pairs (head, tail, relation) by integrating discrete relational information with specific temporal data. This study introduces a dual low-rank embedding framework that unifies temporal patterns and knowledge structures by integrating two modules: a head entity embedding utilizing both static patterns (from head entities) and dynamic patterns (from head entities' temporal paths) with a tail entity embedding derived solely from dynamic patterns of tails (from tail entities' temporal paths). This design enables the capture of crucial temporal dependencies among (head, tail) pairs while maintaining lightweight, efficient graph representations. Furthermore, the proposed framework is model-agnostic, as it can be integrated with various TKI architectures to enhance their inference accuracy. Extensive experiments on established TKI benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating superior performance in infTKI tasks compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

In this study, we examine the influence of sound generated at the ground in inhomogeneous ground-air acoustic wave scenarios. Our analysis reveals ground sound as an effect resulting from the radial component of the inhomogeneous field, which is essential both for meeting the divergence condition for the acoustic tensor and for fulfilling boundary conditions at the ground. This component becomes negligible when the ground's spatial variability is weaker than that imposed by the cylindrical geometric spreading effect. We demonstrate this using a model of a point source positioned above a flat, non-isotropic ground that exhibits both diurnal temperature variations and roughness, as well as its associated variability.

This study provides a complete and non-contradictory demonstration of bipartite Bell nonlocality in a scenario involving two qubits and two measurement settings, specifically for all entangled states. Notably, this demonstration requires neither the determination of an optimal local hidden variable model nor the identification of optimal correlations, allowing the bi-partition of the Bell-Chsh inequality to be bi-partitioned in a novel way to establish nonlocality for all entangled states. Furthermore, this methodology extends to higher-dimensional systems and an increased number of observers, offering a general framework for defining non-contradictory ranges of correlations that are unlocatable.

In line localization using linear regression, the standard approach minimizes the sum of the squared orthogonal distances between data points and the fitted line. This method is known as the Total Least Squares (TLS) algorithm. Our work proposes a new algorithm that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line. This corresponds to applying Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) by rotating the coordinate system so the line's direction aligns with a coordinate axis. Because the vertical distance metric in OLS is heavily influenced by the orientation of the reference frame, the TLS algorithm effectively finds the line direction that minimizes the maximum vertical distance across all possible coordinate rotations. We present an algorithm—named Flat Line Detection (FLD)—based on computing this minimum distance using an efficient, vectorized procedure capable of handling one- to multi-dimensional data within $O(N \log N)$ time. This approach is then extended into a robust variant (R-FLD) through the integration of unimodal, bounded density functions. Both the FLD and R-FLD algorithms outperform the classical Invariant Principal Component Analysis (IPCA) approach, demonstrating superior performance against not only the PCA-based method but also the Outlier-PCA approach on a range of synthetic datasets.

The recent experimental findings by Li et al. identified H-B monolayers with Cmcn symmetry, located within a superhydrogen vacancy regime as the most stable configuration, exhibiting strongly enhanced superconductivity. In our study, the crystal structure and stability of these layers were re-examined using a broader search for potential energy surfaces. By incorporating spin polarization and incorporating electron spin into the analysis, we discovered that the Cmcn phase exhibits only feeble or negligible pairing interactions, and crucially, a recent experimental observation revealed that a monolayer exhibiting C2/m symmetry in a non-hydrogen deficient state is in fact more stable than the Ccmn equivalent. Employing first principles methods, we analyzed the superconducting properties of this more stable C2/m phase but found no evidence for significant or robust electron-phonon coupling. Collectively, our results indicate that hydrogen-bearing two-dimensional monolayers may lack the necessary conditions for robust or notable superconductivity.

In shared-memory multiprocessors, cache pollution occurs when concurrent access by multiple processes contaminates the process's private L1 cache line, often necessitating the process to re-fetch that data. This specific issue arises in flattened partitioning schemes whenever a process writes to a memory address located within the cache line of another process. We identify the cache line span—the count of consecutive cache line addresses a process accesses—as the primary determinant for total pollutions. Consequently, we address the problem of optimizing run allocation by examining how to group processes sharing similar spans into distinct runs to minimize total pollutions. Our approach involves formulating this issue as a linear programming task and developing a heuristic algorithm with experimental results that validate the efficacy of both the proposed model and algorithm in real-world settings.

Building on the work of Clozel, Geraghty, Sarnak, and Lapid concerning the Euler–Poincaré characteristic of certain arithmetic manifolds, we extend these concepts to a broader setting using $L$-parameters. We further explore several implications derived from this generalized framework.

Automated driving systems are increasingly being integrated into automotive safety-critical contexts, prompting extensive research into their formal validation. This work presents a novel formal validation framework for a specific fail-operational system on board an automated vehicle. The approach utilizes system-level modeling to represent the complex interactions between a driving system and its dynamic environment, using the B modeling and verification methodology. The validity of this framework is demonstrated by showing how it can be employed to confirm the substantial proofs-of-correctness already established within an industrial-scale, automation level 2 driving safety concept. The presented framework contributes to the evolving methodology for validating large software systems within autonomous safety concepts by enabling the establishment of novel, large-scale software properties and maintaining continuity with existing conceptual properties.

Recent advances in machine learning have enhanced our ability to forecast behaviors in complex systems. We introduce a data-centric approach for grouping dynamical systems based on predicted outcomes, designed specifically for scenarios with high dimensional state spaces and limited training data. Our method combines convolutional autoencoders to compress high-dimensional observations into lower states with a deep regression model for the clustering criteria. We demonstrate the technique using synthetic forced and unforced chaotic attractors, as well as real-world wind speed forecasting. Results show that this data-driven framework yields comparable performance to unsupervised methods that rely on state-space geometry, while effectively operating in extremely high dimensions and requiring no access to the underlying system dynamics.

This paper explores how three dominant approaches in the history and philosophy of science represent Leibniz's infinitesimals—namely, as idealized entities within an alternative calculus, as the set of zero-difference sequences, or as mappings defining tangent line contact on a curve. The authors argue that examining Leibniz's methodology offers a valuable new perspective on the development of differential and integral calculus during the 18th century and beyond, supplementing existing accounts with fresh insights.

We apply the disturbance theory framework to estimate noise and various error sources for hydrogen intensity mapping observed via interferometers. The total root-mean-square (RMS) noise aligns with standard single-sideband formulas, whereas sources contributing to the RMS error budget depend strongly on k-space weighting, observation geometry, and resolution. Our calculations cover an error budget for a proposed experiment targeting hydrogen at z = 2.25 with angular resolution of 2.2 arcminutes, covering 2.5 square degrees, and utilizing a total of 1000 antenna-hours. We find that after accounting for k-space effects, foreground contamination becomes the primary error term rather than noise, necessitating foreground subtraction. We evaluate this subtraction using a mode filtering method and demonstrate through simulations that it achieves sufficient foreground removal while introducing minimal additional variance.

In quantum field theory, field operators are characterized as carrying infinite momentum extent or being "non-normalizable" due to their underlying mathematical structure. This paper demonstrates a network of equivalent conditions, including operator asymptotic behavior, that clarify these statements and provide rigorous criteria to determine whether they hold. Notably, we derive a distinct spectral condition linked to the momentum spectrum which an individual field's operator must satisfy to exhibit this particular asymptotic property.

Recent advancements in information technology have made it increasingly difficult for users to navigate vast collections of digital content, such as news articles, academic papers, and web pages. While these items may seem overwhelming to individual users, they often present even greater challenges for people with visual impairments, particularly those employing screen readers who cannot visually scan content to determine the best navigation path. To address this issue, we devised a recommender system designed to assist users, including those using assistive technologies, in effectively browsing extensive digital repositories. This proposed hybrid model integrates both document context analysis and user behavior analysis. Furthermore, we introduced specific improvements to refine the system's accuracy. Comprehensive tests conducted on DUCIR, a comprehensive database of scientific publications, demonstrated that our method significantly improves both recommendation and exclusion capabilities, with our approach outperforming a strong baseline collaborative filtering algorithm.

This study establishes that, under appropriate assumptions, asymptotic free Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GNE) matrices are generically of type B when viewed as subalgebras of large random matrices. Previously, Bardoux, Duflo, and Speicher (2015) proved these type A matrices appear generically for type A or type B subalgebras in their works on higher cumulants; however, an explicit construction of the relevant higher moments for the type B case remained elusive. This paper addresses that gap by explicitly computing the higher moments for the type B configuration. The authors leverage an expression of type B free entropy derived from Bardoux, Spechger, and others, applying it alongside recent findings on the openness of the type B freeness relation to finalize their demonstration.

Typically, verification methods involving observations are developed to determine whether a system fulfills a property that can be directly detected through its output sequence of states. Assuming an effective procedure exists to verify property satisfaction by a reference model, the central challenge becomes whether this capability can be extended to systems that are only accessible through state sampling at specified time intervals—what we term a "timed system." This work revives the long-standing algorithm proposed by Knuf and Knuf and Manfredi for the monitor construction of finite transition systems under temporal constraints. The authors present a streamlined algorithm with a more concise proof, thereby enhancing both clarity and computational efficiency.

The LHCb collaboration recently reported on the $\bar{B}_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)\bar{f}_0(980)$ decay channel, where an $a_0(980)\bar{f}_0(980)$ mass spectrum along with the corresponding S-wave phase shifts were presented. In this study, we employ the Bethe-Salpeter formalism to calculate the $a_0(980)\bar{f}_0(980)$ component of this process using a framework that strictly adheres to unitarity. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these findings for the structural nature of the $a_0(980)$ resonance.

The ESO GRAVITY instrument is an interferometric differential astrometry tool at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) capable of achieving sub-mas precision. Its four independent optical channels, each utilizing Mode-Enhanced Spectropolarimetry (MSE) fiber optics, allow it to identify and correct fast, instrument-induced variations in amplitude and phase to gather reliable intensity and differential astrometry data. This approach enables the effective use of on-the-fly observing strategies. To validate this method, the four GRAVITY channels were tested under diverse conditions, leading to significant enhancements in the MSE fiber system's performance. We present here the performance evaluation of GRAVITY by analyzing the stability and flatness of its individual channel responses, as well as consistency in amplitude and astrometric measurements using a standard star.

This paper focuses on solving multivariate polynomial systems where coefficient errors may occur. Existing methods typically assume a global error limit, yet our approach handles scenarios where individual errors exceed this threshold by utilizing the total number of mistakes as our constraint. A fundamental analytical model for the equation of state of non-degenerate plasma is examined, demonstrating its superior simplicity and robustness over existing approaches. The validity of this model is confirmed through rigorous testing in the extreme limits of ideal and complete ionization, as well as in the complex, nonlinear regime of partial ionization. To demonstrate its precision and simplicity, the findings were verified in the non-trivial range where ionization fluctuates significantly.

This work explores the spectral properties of light vector mesons within a (3+1)-dimensional hot medium exhibiting chiral asymmetry, leveraging Holographic Dualities based on a modified AdS/black hole geometry that incorporates a Chern-Sicenses term at its boundary. By analyzing the calculated mass spectrum, we observe a reduction in both light vector meson masses and the corresponding states with higher spin under conditions of increased fermional chirality. These findings suggest a degeneracy between left and right components, hinting at a environment where spontaneous chiral symmetry restoration occurs.

This study introduces a method for estimating key network metrics—including degree distribution, average path length, and clustering coefficient—in large-scale networks. The proposed framework is applicable to small-world networks and tolerates up to $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ Byzantine adversarial nodes. The analysis reveals that sampling the degree distribution of a degree-squared truncated version of the original network yields an accurate estimation of its largest eigenvalue, a finding that directly enables effective path length and clustering calculations. The work establishes these results with high probability using $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ communication bits and $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ rounds, providing $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-sided single-shotted estimates with very high accuracy.

Numerous methods exist for solving the Einstein constraint equations, yet none are universally applicable. This paper introduces a new method, CTTK, built upon a variation of the conformal transverse traceless decomposition combined with an iterative scheme. This approach was used to solve the constraints for two cases: Cauchy data representing head-on collisions of unequal-mass black holes with spin, and an axisymmetric gravitational wave source on a flat background. In both instances, the data generation code achieved single-precision performance of approximately 100 Mflops per second per CPU core and demonstrated the capacity to converge to a high relative accuracy of $10^{-12}$ or lower.

The future Jiangmen Neutrino Observatory (JNOO), or JUNO, is a liquid scintillator experiment designed to investigate reactor neutrinos. Its core is a massive spherical vessel 20 meters in diameter filled with liquid scintillator, surrounded by some 5,000 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) mounted on an inner support structure. These 20-inch diameter large-size PMTs, sourced primarily from Hamamatsu, are engineered specifically to operate within JUNO's low-field scintillation medium. A defining requirement for this project is achieving uniform sensitivity across the entire PMK batch, a standard met by screening each unit under JUNO-relevant conditions using an automated system that measures sensitivity and dark rate. This paper outlines the specific test setup and sensitivity screening methodology, presenting initial data from a small sample of PMKs that validates excellent consistency in sensitivity, with 98.8% of units falling between 0.90 and 1.10 times the reference PMK's sensitivity.

Predicting multivariate time series is essential across numerous fields, yet it remains difficult due to nonlinear dynamics and long-term dependencies. Although existing methods have made progress, there is a lack of models that can automatically infer graph structures from data while effectively handling these temporal challenges. To address this, we introduce AGCN, an adaptive graph convolutional network that merges current spatial-temporal convolutions with a neural mechanism for structural learning. First, it constructs an initial graph by mapping time series features to nodes in a k-nearest neighbor (KNN) learning vector quantization framework. Subsequently, it dynamically learns and refines both the nodes and edges of the graph through convolutional operations to align with specific time steps. The core innovation, a nodes-and-edges unit, allows the graph topology to adapt to different contexts within the time series, distinguishing this approach from existing methods that typically keep static structures. Experimental results on eight datasets demonstrate that AGCN significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in prediction accuracy and offers a distinct advantage over existing auto-regressive autoencoders, which often fail to recover graph structures that adequately reflect the underlying data distribution.

Knowledge distillation has proven highly effective, with recent strategies focusing on integrating multiple teachers via ensemble averaging of logits. Nevertheless, these methods often suffer from logits inconsistency and teacher divergence, particularly when training teachers on separate datasets that lack a uniform distribution. This paper introduces Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel knowledge distillation approach designed to produce robust student models by faithfully distilling critical information from various teachers. PILE creates a unified, generalized student training framework through a systematic pairwise comparison of teacher pairs. Specifically, it defines a loss function representing the distance between an individual teacher and the aggregated consensus of all others, which emphasizes the teachers' common knowledge while filtering out their specific discrepancies. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of PILE over existing state-of-the-art ensemble ensemble techniques, confirming its ability to effectively capture teacher consensus without the noise inherent in raw averaging.

We investigate Basis Pursuit within a continuum setting and establish a theorem characterizing when unique solutions exist. This characterization is then utilized to demonstrate the uniqueness of Basis Pursuit when applied to radial basis function networks with Gaussian kernels on a sphere, given sufficient node density. The result further proves uniqueness for the related Kernel Ridge Network as the regularization parameter approaches infinity. To support uniqueness proofs, we introduce a broader class of problems: minimizing the sum of a semi-norm on a vector space and a lower semi-continuous function defined on a direct sum of that space and a continuum. Uniqueness criteria for this general case are established through features of the subdifferential. These findings rely heavily on onextremally complete spaces, a concept that supersedes previously used strictly convex or reflexive assumptions to ensure unique solution uniqueness.

The P4 language has emerged as the leading choice for programming switch-remodelable network devices, notably the BNOB series by Barefoot Networks (now NVIDIA Networking), a flexible, resource-managed P16 architecture featuring matched tables. To support research into this specific hardware implementation, this paper introduces the P4 compiler backend, a key component of an open-source toolchain. Developed in collaboration with Barefoot, P4L provides the necessary infrastructure to translate high-level code into low-level bitstrings tailored for their hardware. This process involves a multi-phase strategy: transforming match-extract tables into TGVM-based implementations, handling queueing systems, and mapping action executions to specific architectural elements.

Accurate solutions to the vector transport equation on lowest-order Raviart-RT tetrahedral elements are typically achieved using a mass-conserving mass matrix. However, extending this scheme to quadrilateral patches introduces a mismatch in the mass matrix that significantly reduces numerical accuracy. This study introduces a method to construct a precise, consensual mass matrix for these essential quadrilateral elements, thereby enabling the application of the successful FV-FE technique. The exactness of this derived matrix is demonstrated through its use with FV-FE methods to solve the vector transport equation.

Federated learning (FL) has established itself as a robust paradigm for secure machine learning, yet the extent to which standard FL mechanisms guarantee fairness or privacy remains uncertain. This study introduces fairness assessments for centralized FL and demonstrates that inherent biases can emerge across federated components, with non-differential privacy-protected FL systems producing models that replicate non-stochastic, privately trained counterparts. We further examine two dominant privacy preservation techniques— Differential Privacy (DP) and Perturbation—and reveal a counterintuitive finding: both can exhibit bias even when applied to private data, meaning higher privacy levels do not necessarily ensure fairer outcomes. Leveraging these insights, we propose Bias-aware Federations (BAF), a BAF that remains invariant regardless of the underlying privacy preservation method. Empirical tests on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate this theoretical framework and support the BAF implementation. Ultimately, our work highlights a critical research gap, urging the machine learning community to address fairness within the FL landscape more systematically.

Model parallel deep neural networks are frequently employed to train large-scale architectures, enabling the processing of even more extensive datasets by distributing both computational layers and training data across multiple regions. Increasing the number of these geographic areas allows for greater memory capacity, though it introduces additional areas that must be synchronized, thereby amplifying communication overhead. This added latency can significantly diminish training velocity. This paper introduces a new technique, called Regional Critic Training (RCT), which reduces such communication costs by enabling each region to learn independently. Under specific theoretical conditions, it has been demonstrated that R maintains compatibility with existing distributed training methods. Experimental results indicate not only greater flexibility in hardware placement but also a substantial improvement in training efficiency compared to conventional model parallelism.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering systems can generate a Wada property, wherein boundary sets shared among distinct attractors are entirely encompassed by a single fractal attractor. In these systems, Wada boundaries involve at least three separate attractors and cannot exist in three-dimensional space without the inclusion of a fourth. While three-dimensional incompressible Hamiltonian systems can theoretically exhibit Wada basins, this capability is exclusive to compressive systems when dissipative forces are present. This study investigates how weak dissipation influences the dynamics of three-dimensional scattering near Lyapunov instabilities, specifically looking for conditions that induce a transition from regular to chaotic behavior and result in the emergence of Wada basins. The results indicate that weak dissipative fields both generate the necessary Wada basin topology and significantly enlarge the parameter domain in which basins extend. Furthermore, the fraction of the initial phase space affected by these expanded Wada basins grows with increasing dissipation strength up to a specific threshold beyond which the system fully escapes chaotic scattering.

We examine a model featuring three right-handed neutrinos, which account for baryogenesis via the flavor-changing mechanism. Although this framework was previously analyzed, it has been shown to generate the required baryon asymmetry through leptogenesis if the intermediate mass scales are slightly modified; this same adjustment allows the model to evade current LHC constraints. Consequently, we calculate the physical parameters responsible for the intermediate mass scales and investigate the resulting Higgs couplings to di-neutrino pairs. Our analysis demonstrates that these light particles induce di-neutrino couplings that are orders of magnitude stronger than those for Standard Model neutrinos, a model characteristic that facilitates baryogenesis. Furthermore, we outline how these weak di-neutrino couplings could be detected at a high-luminosity electron-positron collider.

Activity recognition in videos is a fundamental computer vision challenge with broad applications ranging from video indexing and search to human-computer interaction. Existing solutions typically employ hierarchical architectures featuring an encoder for extracting features and a recognizer for identifying specific actions. Current methods often utilize global pooling on spatial convolutional features to achieve invariance to motion timing, duration, and frequency. In contrast, this paper presents a more efficient alternative by replacing global pooling with a Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN). Anchored on the assumption that action occurrences cluster within distinct temporal intervals, the proposed HAN learns to focus on these intervals while aggregating feature maps from a convolutional encoder into overlapping temporal windows. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this method surpasses traditional global pooling and other attention-based baseline models in the temporal encoding phase. Furthermore, the framework exhibits robustness regarding the temporal support for action execution, maintaining stable performance even with varying lengths of informative data.

This review examines how interstellar clouds form and evolve, a dynamic influenced by gravity, magnetic fields, magnetic flux, magnetic support, thermal pressure, turbulence, contraction, collapse, fragmentation, and accretion. These processes determine a cloud's structure and its eventual stellar output in terms of quantity, timing, mass distribution, spatial layout, and internal characteristics. Monitoring biological motion is essential for both human perception and the functional operations of robotic vision systems. While detecting such movement computationally is straightforward for static cameras, capturing it from handheld devices like webcams, web cameras, or DVRs presents considerable difficulty. This study examines a computational method designed to identify biological motion within videos recorded by handheld cameras. The core of this method is a movement model that separates the video content into three components: hand movement, body translation, and camera rotation, all of which generate apparent feature displacement. The system determines the most probable path through visual search, evaluating how well it matches the input video. The feasibility of this model is demonstrated by generating simulated video data from a virtual human performing actions, assuming specific camera movements driven by a simulated operator. The calculated likelihood of these simulated sequences is then verified using real recorded footage.

Optimizing electricity grid management is vital for ensuring efficient and effective grid operation. We investigate this issue by applying quantum algorithms to optimize grid power distribution. We begin by outlining the problem and introducing its formulation via Optimization Theory's Theory Most Recent Theorem, subsequently defining its quantum state vector representation. Subsequently, we implement the Larsen et al. (2019) algorithm to optimize an test electricity network. Finally, we present and compare our results with traditional methods, demonstrating that the Larsen et al. (2019) approach achieves grid optimization using fewer computational resources compared to classical optimization techniques while delivering results of equal precision.

Modern machine learning methods for extracting physical laws from data have seen rapid development across all stages of the data-driven physics pipeline: discovery, validation, and interpretation. These approaches, grounded in neural networks and other ML models, have yielded significant insights into areas like high-energy physics, astrophysics, and fluid dynamics. Nevertheless, the transferability of these techniques to various physics subfields remains inconsistent, highlighting fundamental discrepancies. As a result, we evaluate state-of-the-art extraction methods against three core scientific objectives—evaluating their capacity to (1) generalize across datasets, (2) uncover causal mechanisms, and (3) facilitate human understanding. This evaluation establishes a framework for identifying necessary future research, including the potential universal laws of physics that ML must detect and the systematic barriers limiting current applications.

This analysis details a search conducted by the ATLAS detector at the LHC for pair-produced heavy, electrically charged particles with masses exceeding 100 GeV/c² and lifetimes longer than 1 cm, specifically looking for those that decay within the inner detector. Data from the full Run 2 run, recorded by ATLAS at 13 TeV proton-proton collision energy, are examined. Because these long-lived particles exhibit a significant reduction in specific ionization as they lose momentum, they often evade standard searches for such entities, which is why we employ a dedicated methodology. This study reports no significant signal; thus, we establish 95% confidence level upper limits on particle production cross-sections. These constraints cover charged colored particles, such as single production or specifically 1/3 fractional charged states, as well as particles with integer charge.

We present near-unity efficacy on-chip single-photon sources, achieved by ridge waveguide integrated with InGaAs quantum dots. By measuring the electrical excitation efficacy—a key metric representing the probability of generating a photon per absorbed pump photon—at 1.55 micrometers, we achieved 0.83 ± 0.04, representing the highest results to date for this wavelength range. Combined with previously established near 100% fidelity and >99% purity, these high efficacy rates enabled the demonstration of an overall source efficacy of 0.98 ± 0.03 (under 1% uncertainty) via 1.7 μm wavelength time-resolved single-photon counting. This total efficacy accounts for the intrinsic source contribution, collection efficiency, and on-chind coupling losses. These performance metrics establish a functional, integrated single-photon source suitable for practical quantum information applications.

Inelastic neutron scattering studies reveal that the boson peak cannot be explained by a single simple model. While scattering intensity displays a linear q-dependence in many glass systems, a significant q-zero slope is observed in others. These variations cannot be resolved using a Debye model, as both system types share identical low-temperature thermal expansion behaviors, ruling out a Debye vibrational spectrum. Instead, a generalized continuum hypothesis provides a consistent framework for most systems, with a single parameter set capable of fitting the q-zero slope across varying q ranges. However, this continuum model fails to fit the q-dependence seen in systems exhibiting a strong boson peak. Instead, a two-level system model effectively captures these results. It is possible that a hybrid vibration model combining elements of both the two-level system and generalized continuum hypotheses will eventually describe all phenomena.

Supernovae, astrophysical jets, and high-energy cosmic-ray sources illuminate the universe, with their radiative intensity governed by eigenchannels that dictate energy deposition modes in these systems. Although recent advances have enabled detailed 3D radiative hydrodynamic simulations, critical constraints remain: these simulations rely on multigroup approximations that partition radiation into discrete groups, thereby missing radiation transport phenomena occurring between groups. To address this limitation, we develop radiative transfer simulations employing accurate radiation-hydrodynamic coupling and introduce sum principles derived from the eigenchannels. These principles serve as diagnostic tools to evaluate simulation accuracy while providing a roadmap for enhancing computational fidelity.

The solution landscape of many multi-objective optimization problems contains substantial diversity, far exceeding what standard algorithms typically discover, often resulting in a main Pareto front supplemented by numerous sub-optimal layers. Although there is a growing interest in measuring solution phenotypic diversity, existing methods frequently fail to capture full diversity due to limitations in robustness, spatial coverage, and computational efficiency. This paper introduces a new multi-criteria approach for understanding and diversifying solution distribution spaces, offering a balanced method that is both locally and globally robust while maintaining high efficiency. Furthermore, the authors evaluate the proposed metrics across various test problems to demonstrate their effectiveness and availability for future comparative studies on diversity assessment.

Valley physics in two-dimensional (2D) systems has garnered significant interest due to the capacity for distinct electronic behaviors within a single layer, a property enabled by valley degrees of freedom. While spin-phonon interactions have historically been pivotal in spintronics, the coupling between valley states and phonons is typically a weak perturbation. This study utilizes ab initio many-body perturbation theory to examine electron-phonon coupling (EPC) near K/K' points in selected 2D materials, revealing that certain mechanisms—specifically deformation potential, long-range piezoelectric, and long-range strain-induced magnetic—can profoundly impact valley dynamics through substantial EPC strength. Reassessing previous density functional theory findings with many-body methods alters the predicted ranking of K/K' point effects in MoS₂. Furthermore, we identify EPC variations orders of magnitude stronger at the K/K' points compared to other regions in FeGe and BiGe monolayers, resulting from long-range strain-induced magnetic interactions; these materials therefore exhibit robust valley responses to strain and audio-frequency vibrations due to intense EPC.
